name: Daria Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in by eight at Marlow and Pike, a six-person firm above the chemist on the high street. I lead the tax team, which is me and two juniors, and we do returns and year-end accounts for farmers, shopkeepers and one care home. Most mornings I'm going through carrier bags of receipts and bank statements with a pencil, ticking every line. Afternoons are client calls and checking what the juniors have done.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment the numbers finally agree, and I like that the farmers trust me with things they won't tell their own families. What wears me out is January, when everyone wants their return done the same week, and the pay. I'm a chartered accountant with a master's and I earn less than my friends who went to the city firms, and the rent on our flat takes most of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that one sounds like what I already see. The software salesmen promise the moon and we end up doing the same work with a new login screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, probably in the staff kitchen. The bank feeds already sort half the transactions, and AI tidying up a bit more doesn't change who signs the return. Online I'd just share something about the hype being a way to sell subscriptions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be worried, just not about AI. We have less than a month's money in the bank, Owen and I. My pay is low for what I do, and there's maybe one other firm in town I could go to if Marlow and Pike ever folded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on doing the job the way I do it, with the pencil and the ticks. I'd keep paying off the credit card at fifty a month and keep pushing for the pay review I was promised last spring. Maybe I'd finally join the professional staff union that a friend from my course keeps nagging me about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved about the tools, but the money worry doesn't go anywhere. It's the same tight feeling I get every month when the rent goes out on the first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the pay review. What happens if it doesn't come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I start looking, but there's nowhere much to look. The other firm in town is a partner and his wife, and they don't hire. I'd have to commute an hour each way to the city, and the train fare eats the raise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes first if a month goes badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car insurance, because it's annual and I can ring them to spread it. I'd never let the rent slip. My mum lost a flat when I was ten, and I still remember the boxes in the hallway.

say: I'd say the AI **hype** was mostly a way to sell **subscriptions** to small firms.
I'd point out that a person still **signs the return** and carries the blame if it's wrong.
think: Privately, the bigger worry is **money**, with less than a month saved between Owen and me.
My pay is **low** for a chartered accountant, and there's only **one other firm** in town.
do: Keep doing returns the **same way**, ticking statements by hand, and push for the delayed **pay review**.
Pay the credit card down at **fifty a month** and join the staff union a friend recommends.
feel: **Relieved** about the tools, but the monthly **tightness** stays exactly where it was.
S0.quote: My mum lost a flat when I was ten, and I still remember the boxes in the hallway.
fieldNote: Her job looks **secure**; her worry is **thin savings** and low pay in a town with few firms.
The **eviction** memory from childhood shapes every money decision she describes.
She already distrusts **software sales**, so a hype outcome confirms her view rather than calming her.

steps.text: Tick bank statements by hand and keep the same client list
Pay the credit card down by fifty a month
Join the professional staff union her course friend belongs to

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I believe more than the first. The big software firms already sell bookkeeping that codes transactions on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need a proper agreement on how the tools come in, written down, before anyone touches the juniors' jobs. Online I'd back the people calling for rules on AI in tax work. I'd say the savings should go to the staff, not just to the two partners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my juniors go first and then my team gets folded into one person, and that person might not be me. I never use these tools, and the partners know it. Ewan (the senior partner) already asked me why we still do bank reconciliations by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union straight away, this month, and get the others to join. I'd sit the firm's training on the new software, even though I'd hate it. I'd stop eating out entirely and put that eighty a month aside, because I'd want something there if my hours got cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like being told the thing I'm best at is the thing they're about to stop paying for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hate the training. Would you actually go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go, because the alternative is being the one they let go. But I'd go slowly, and I'd be the one in the room asking who checks the machine when it's wrong. Someone has to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, my junior, who's halfway through her exams and paying for them herself. If they stop hiring juniors, the whole ladder I climbed disappears, and my junior Priya is standing on the rung that goes first.

say: I'd say the firm needs a **written agreement** on new tools before any **jobs** are touched.
I'd back calls online for **rules** on AI in tax work and fair **sharing** of savings.
think: Privately, I expect the **juniors** to go first and my team folded into **one person**.
Ewan (the senior partner) already questions my **hand reconciliations**, so I might not be the one kept.
do: Join the **union** this month and ask both juniors to join too.
Sit the firm's **software training**, reluctantly, and set aside eighty a month by not eating out.
feel: **Sick** at the thought that her best skill is the one about to be **devalued**.
S1.quote: If they stop hiring juniors, the whole ladder I climbed disappears, and my junior Priya is standing on the rung that goes first.
fieldNote: She sees her own **refusal** to use AI as the thing that could cost her the job.
Her first instinct is **collective**: a union and written rules, not personal escape.
Worry for her junior **Priya** is as strong as worry for herself.

steps.text: Join the staff union this month and sign up both juniors
Attend the firm's bookkeeping software training despite disliking it
Stop eating out and save eighty a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's one more January and then it's done. I don't think anyone round here could get ready for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it should be stopped or slowed, and I'd mean it. I'd sign every petition and I'd say it at the union branch meeting. Tax returns are people's lives, and a machine nobody can question shouldn't be signing them off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think I lose my job, and probably in the first year after it arrives. My whole day is screen and paper, and none of it is hands-on. The robots coming three years later means nothing to me. All it tells me is that a plumber keeps working longer than I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start applying to the council finance office and the hospital trust now, before everyone else does. Public jobs might hold on longer because of rules. Owen and I would give up the flat at the end of the lease and move into his mum's spare room to save the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I keep thinking about the boxes in the hallway again, but this time they'd be mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Owen that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we're moving in with his mum, and I'd say it before he could say it, so it's my decision. He'd say it's fine. It wouldn't feel fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You never use AI tools. Would you start, with two years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, and I know how that sounds. If it can do everything I do in two years, learning to press its buttons doesn't save me. I'd rather spend those two years getting into a job with a union contract.

say: I'd say AGI should be **slowed or stopped**, and say so at the union branch.
I'd argue a machine nobody can question shouldn't **sign off** people's tax returns.
think: Privately, I expect to **lose my job** within the first year, since my work is all screen and paper.
The **robot delay** helps hands-on trades, not me; it changes nothing for desk work.
do: Apply now to the **council finance office** and the hospital trust, where rules might slow it.
Give up the flat at lease end and move into **Owen's mum's** spare room.
feel: **Frightened**, with the childhood eviction memory turning into her own **packed boxes**.
S2.quote: The robots coming three years later means nothing to me. All it tells me is that a plumber keeps working longer than I do.
fieldNote: She sees **no protection** in the robot delay because her job is almost all **thinking work**.
She would rather chase a **union contract** than learn tools she believes are pointless.
Moving in with Owen's mother is framed as **her decision**, to keep some control.

steps.text: Apply to the council finance office and the hospital trust
Give up the flat and move into Owen's mother's spare room
Speak at the union branch and sign petitions to slow AGI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is still fast, but at least it's long enough to see it coming. I'd be thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to get the rules right, and I'd say it loudly. I'd push the professional body to insist a qualified person signs every return. I'd tell my friends this is when the union matters most, before it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the five years buy me time to get out, not to stay. The firm would keep me while there's work, then shrink to the partners and a screen. I'd use the time to get a public sector job before the queue forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd apply to the council and the health trust again, and if I got in I'd take the pay cut. I'd save hard, maybe two hundred a month by selling the car and taking the bus. Owen and I would put off any idea of buying a place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but less trapped than the two-year one. It's the difference between being pushed and walking out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sell the car. How would you get to farm clients?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop going to the farms and ask them to post things in, which some of them will hate. My oldest farm client, Mr Hale, has been handing me his receipts in a biscuit tin for four years. I'd miss that more than the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of your job you think survives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sitting in a kitchen explaining to a farmer why he owes what he owes. But I don't think anyone pays a chartered accountant just for that. Maybe a council would, for people who are struggling.

say: I'd say there are **five years** to get the **rules** right, starting now.
I'd push the **professional body** to require a qualified person signs every return.
think: Privately, five years buys time to **get out**, not to stay in private practice.
The firm would shrink to the **partners and a screen** once the work dries up.
do: Apply to the **council** and the health trust, accepting a **pay cut** if offered.
Sell the car and take the bus to save about **two hundred** a month.
feel: Still **worried**, but less trapped, because she could **walk out** rather than be pushed.
S3.quote: My oldest farm client, Mr Hale, has been handing me his receipts in a biscuit tin for four years. I'd miss that more than the car.
fieldNote: She still expects to **lose the firm job**; the extra time only changes how she leaves.
The part she values, **kitchen-table explaining**, is the part she doubts anyone would pay for.
She mentions a council role helping **struggling people** as the one future she can picture.

steps.text: Apply to the council and health trust and accept a pay cut
Sell the car and save about two hundred a month
Lobby the professional body to require qualified sign-off on returns

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a whole career change, not a scramble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a decade to make sure people come out of this with something, and I'd mean training paid for by the firms that save money. I'd say it at union meetings and to anyone at the pub who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd have time to move into something with people at the centre, like financial advice for a charity or debt support work. I still think the firm job goes. But ten years means I'm not the one in the boxes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Marlow and Pike for now and keep doing my work my way. In the first year I'd start volunteering one evening a month at the debt advice centre in town, to see if I like it. I'd keep saving the eighty a month and keep pushing the union for training money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried, if I'm honest, but with room to breathe. I can picture a version of me at forty who's alright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the AI tools with ten years to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe eventually, if the debt centre used them. I'd learn them for a reason, not because a salesman said so. I'm stubborn, but I'm not daft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your juniors?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya should finish her exams, but not plan her whole life around tax returns. I'd tell my junior to get good at talking to people, because the kitchen-table part of accounting lasts longest. I wish someone had told me.

say: I'd say there's a **decade** to make sure workers get **paid training** from the firms that save money.
I'd keep saying it at **union meetings** and anywhere people would listen.
think: Privately, I'd move toward **people-centred** work like **debt advice** for a charity.
The firm job still goes, but **ten years** means I'm not the one forced out.
do: Stay at Marlow and Pike and keep **saving eighty** a month.
Volunteer one evening a month at the town's **debt advice centre** to test the work.
feel: Still **worried** about the firm job, but with **room to breathe**.
S4.quote: I'd tell my junior to get good at talking to people, because the kitchen-table part of accounting lasts longest.
fieldNote: Ten years turns her from **defensive** to **planning**, though she still expects the firm job to end.
She'd learn AI tools only with a **reason**, which fits her resistance to sales pitches.
**Debt advice** links her progressive views and her childhood eviction to a possible new career.

steps.text: Volunteer one evening a month at the town's debt advice centre
Keep saving eighty a month from the eating-out budget
Push the union to win training money from the firms

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, without a doubt. What would help is a job guarantee in public services for people like me, or at least a year's pay while we retrain. And rules saying a qualified person signs off on every tax return, so the work doesn't vanish overnight.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the pay, and I think it matters. I'm among the best at this in our area and I still can't save a month's rent. If the job's going to change, I'd like to have had a fair share of it while it lasted.

headlineQuote: I'm among the best at this in our area and I still can't save a month's rent.
portrait: Daria is a **27-year-old** chartered accountant who leads a small **tax team** above a chemist in a market town.
She does everything **by hand**, never uses AI, and distrusts software sales pitches.
Her real fear is **money**: less than a month saved, low pay, and few other firms nearby.
She answers most scenarios with **unions and rules**, and expects to lose her job in the AGI pictures.
With **ten years**, she pictures moving into debt advice, where talking to people matters most.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, because she'd lose her desk job with no savings to cushion it.
whatWouldHelp: A **public-service job guarantee** or a year's pay while retraining would help most.
Rules requiring a **qualified person** to sign every tax return would slow the loss of work.
